newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik hostage talks start after three-hour delay.
newsitem.headline: Tajik hostage talks start after three-hour delay.

text.p: Tajikistan's president began face-to-face negotiations with a rebel Islamic group on Monday to discuss the fate of six foreign and local hostages, a Western diplomat said.
He said two members of the rebel group had arrived in the eastern Tajik town of Obigarm after a three-hour delay to meet Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov.
Prospects for the captives' release -- already promised after the government surrended a group of rebel fighters and arms to the group on Friday -- were unclear, the diplomat said.

Russia's Itar-Tass news agency said the rebels arrived at the talks with one of the hostages, Tajik Security Minister Saidamir Zukhurov. It was not clear where the five other hostages were and Tajik officials were not immediately available to comment.

Apart from Zukhurov, the rebel group led by brothers Bakhrom and Rizvon Sadirov is holding two United Nations military observers -- a Swiss and a Ukrainian -- and three representatives of the U.N. refugee agency.
Government officials in this Central Asian state say they have received promises from the Sadirovs that the hostages will not be harmed and will be released after the talks with Rakhmonov.

But the rebels had also previously pledged to release all the captives after the Tajik authorities allowed more than 30 armed fighters to reach Sadirov's base on Saturday. Only some of the hostages were released.

The crisis erupted on February 4, when Bakhrom Sadirov's rebel group seized the first of the hostages and demanded that the government give free passage for his brother Rizvon and 40 supporters to join him from Afghanistan.
On Monday, the president arrived at Obigarm, 80 km (50 miles) east of the capital Dushanbe, by 9 a.m (0400 GMT), an official said.

The delegation traveling with Rakhmonov for talks was unusually senior for hostage negotations, and included the country's deputy prime minister, the defence minister and his deputy, and other officials, Tass said.

"Bakhrom said he was ready to negotiate directly with the president and the president readily accepted the proposal," Rakhmonov's spokesman Zafar Saidov said on Sunday, adding that the rebel leader gave assurances the hostages would not be harmed.
"Don't worry about the hostages. Nothing threatens their lives," he quoted Bakhrom Sadirov as saying.
But the two Tajik sides have little trust in each other and it was only the intervention of Russia which led to negotiations resulting in earlier releases of some hostages.
Russia, which views Tajikistan as a barrier against the spread of Islamic fundamentalism, has a considerable military force there and helps police its border with Afghanistan.
Moscow backs Rakhmonov, both politically and economically, and has considerable influence over his government.
